usage: Standard polite call for help to anyone, strangers included
반말, shouted to a close friend or family member
Softer, more formal request when there's no immediate danger
누가 (someone) added when calling out to a crowd
examples: 도와주세요! 도와주세요!
Help! Help me!
Shouted twice in rapid succession — the bare repeated cry that draws attention fast in a crowd
A: 가방을 못 들겠어요. 좀 도와주세요. / B: 네, 잠깐만요!
A: I can't lift this bag. Please help me. / B: Sure, just a moment!
Everyday non-emergency use; 좀 softens the request to 'a little help'
할머니가 쓰러지셨어요! 누가 좀 도와주세요!
My grandmother collapsed! Somebody please help!
Real crisis; 누가 scans the crowd, and 쓰러지셨어요 uses honorific because the person is an elder
nuance: 도와주세요 is built from the irregular verb 돕다 (to help) + -아/어 주세요 (please do for me), so the stem changes: 돕- → 도와, giving 도와주세요, literally 'please do the helping for me'. In a true emergency you shout it bare and loud; for ordinary favors you soften with 좀 ('just a little') or upgrade to 도와주시겠어요? to sound polite rather than panicked. The 반말 form 도와줘 is strictly for close friends or younger family — shouting it at a stranger reads as rude even under stress. The nearest life-or-death alternative is 살려 주세요 ('please keep me alive'), but that crosses the line into mortal peril; for anything from a stuck zipper to a medical scare, 도와주세요 covers it. English speakers often say just '도움!' (the noun 'help/aid'), which isn't a cry for assistance, or bark bare 도와, which sounds like a blunt command — always keep 주세요 to stay both intelligible and polite.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please do the helping for me' — built from 돕다 (to help, irregular ㅂ stem) + 아/어 주세요. The ㅂ changes to 와: 돕- → 도와. The real meaning is an all-purpose cry for help, covering emergencies and everyday favors alike.

존댓말 형태 도와주세요 is safe with anyone — strangers, staff, elders. In genuine danger you shout it bare. For a small everyday request, 좀 도와주세요 or 도와주시겠어요? sounds less panicked. Reserve 반말 도와줘 strictly for close friends or younger family, never a stranger.

살려 주세요 ('please save my life') is the step beyond: use it only when your life is genuinely at risk — drowning, an attacker. For everything from a heavy box to a medical incident, 도와주세요 covers it. 도움을 주시겠어요? is a polite formal phrasing but rarely shouted in crisis.
도와줘 (반말) → 도와주세요 (존댓말) → 좀 도와주세요 (softened) → 도와주시겠어요? (formal request) → 누가 좀 도와주세요! (appeal to a crowd). All share the same 도와- stem.

English speakers shout '도움!' (the noun 'help/aid') — that's not a verb cry. Others drop 주세요 and bark '도와' at a stranger, which sounds like a blunt order. And some mistakenly say '돕아주세요' — wrong: 돕다's ㅂ changes to 와, so it must be 도와주세요.

mistakes: Saying 도움 to mean 'Help!'
도움 is the noun 'help/aid', not a cry. To call for help you need the verb plus 주세요: 도와주세요.
Shouting 도와 to a stranger.
Bare 도와 is a blunt 반말 command that sounds rude under stress. Add 주세요 (도와주세요) for anyone you don't know.
Building it as 도와 주세요 with the wrong stem, e.g. 돕아주세요.
돕다 is irregular: the ㅂ changes to 와, giving 도와주세요, not 돕아주세요. The correct form is 도와주세요.

english: Save me! / Help, I'm in danger!
usage: 존댓말 cry used only in life-threatening danger
반말, screamed to anyone when there's no time for politeness
Fixed set phrase shouted to a crowd; literally 'save a person'
Please, I'm begging you, save me
제발 ('I beg you') added to plead for mercy or to an attacker
examples: 살려 주세요! 살려 주세요!
Save me! Help!
Repeated bare scream when you genuinely fear for your life — the raw sound of mortal terror
A: 물에 빠졌어요! 살려 주세요! / B: 거기 있어요! 지금 가요!
A: I'm drowning! Save me! / B: Stay there! I'm coming now!
A/B exchange in a water emergency; 빠지다 = 'to fall/sink into'
불이 났는데 못 나가요. 사람 살려!
There's a fire and I can't get out. Somebody help!
Trapped-in-fire scenario; 사람 살려 is the reflexive crowd-alert, shorter and rawer than 살려 주세요
nuance: 살려 주세요 is built from 살리다 (to keep alive, causative of 살다 'to live') + 아/어 주세요, so it literally begs 'please keep me alive' — a step of mortal urgency beyond 도와주세요. You use it only when your life is genuinely at risk: drowning, a physical attack, a fire with no exit. The critical line: 도와주세요 covers any need for help, including danger; 살려 주세요 signals that without intervention you will die or be seriously harmed. Under that level of terror, register collapses — strangers may hear 살려 줘 or the fixed crowd-shout 사람 살려 ('save a person!'), which Koreans produce almost reflexively. 제발 살려 주세요 pleads desperately and is also used when begging an attacker to stop. English speakers most commonly mistranslate 'save me' as 저장해 주세요 (save a file), or reach for 구해 주세요, which is correct but sounds less viscerally desperate than the idiomatic 살려 주세요 / 사람 살려.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please keep me alive' — 살리다 is the causative of 살다 ('to live'), so the request is: cause me to continue living. The real meaning is an absolute emergency plea used only when you believe your life is at immediate risk.

존댓말 살려 주세요 is appropriate even to a stranger in mortal danger. Under extreme fear, 살려 줘 (반말) and the fixed 사람 살려! (ageless crowd cry) both occur naturally. 제발 살려 주세요 is the begging form used toward an attacker. You would never use this for minor trouble — it will alarm everyone within earshot.

도와주세요 vs 살려 주세요: the difference is whether you might die. A heavy suitcase or a medical scare → 도와주세요. Drowning, a mugger, a locked burning room → 살려 주세요. 구해 주세요 also means 'rescue me' and is correct, but 살려 주세요 is more viscerally urgent and idiomatic.
살려 줘 (반말) → 살려 주세요 (존댓말) → 제발 살려 주세요 (desperate pleading) → 사람 살려! (fixed crowd-alarm). 사람 살려 has no politeness level — it's a reflexive shout.

The fatal mistake is 저장해 주세요 — that's 'please save (a file/data)'. To save a life use 살리다: 살려 주세요. 구해 주세요 is also correct but less instinctive to Koreans in a panic. Never use 살려 주세요 for non-life-threatening help — it causes immediate alarm.

mistakes: Using 저장해 주세요 for 'save me'.
저장하다 means to save data/a file. To save a life you need 살리다: 살려 주세요.
Using 살려 주세요 for minor trouble like a heavy box.
It signals mortal danger and will alarm people. For ordinary help say 도와주세요.
Writing 살여 주세요 or 살려주새요.
The stem is 살리- → 살려, and the ending is 주세요 (not 주새요). Correct: 살려 주세요.

usage: The set alarm shout; shouted to everyone regardless of age or formality
존댓말 report to people around you; 나다 = 'to break out'
Fuller, clearer 존댓말 form — best when phoning 119 or reporting calmly
저기 (over there) added to point to the location
examples: 불이야! 불이야! 다 나가요!
Fire! Fire! Everyone get out!
Bare alarm cry paired with 다 나가요 ('everyone leave') — the natural combination that empties a building
A: 불났어요! 빨리 나가세요! / B: 어디요? / A: 저기 주방이요!
A: There's a fire! Get out quickly! / B: Where? / A: Over there, the kitchen!
Real A/B exchange showing how to direct people; 주방 = kitchen
주방에서 불이 났어요. 119에 신고해 주세요! 다들 밖으로 나가세요!
A fire has started in the kitchen. Call 119! Everyone go outside!
Calm full-sentence report to bystanders; 신고하다 = 'report (to authorities)'
nuance: 불이야! is the fixed Korean alarm cry equivalent to English 'Fire!' — 불 (fire) + 이야 (exclamatory copula after a consonant). It is grammatically 반말, but the convention is that anyone shouts this to anyone in a fire emergency because politeness is irrelevant when lives are at risk. Contrast the alarm with the report: 불이야! is what you shout to get people moving; 불이 났어요 or 불났어요 is the calmer explanation you give to a 119 dispatcher or a bystander you're briefing. The verb 나다 ('to break out/occur') is the natural partner: 불이 나다, just as 사고가 나다 — in Korean, fires and accidents 'break out', not 'happen'. English speakers most often say bare '불' (just the noun 'fire/flame') which won't read as an alarm, or try '불 알람!' mixing in English, or attach the post-vowel 야 to get '불야' — but 불 ends in a consonant (ㄹ), so the exclamatory ending must be 이야: 불이야!.

structuredNuance.t: 불 (fire) + 이야 (exclamatory copula after consonant) literally means 'It's fire!' The real function is a mass alarm shout that overrides politeness. Everyone — children, elders, staff — uses this same form in a fire.

불이야! is a register-free alarm — the only situation where 반말 to strangers is fully expected. To report or explain, switch to 불났어요 (casual 존댓말) or 불이 났어요 (fuller 존댓말). When phoning 119, the clear 불이 났어요 with address and floor is what dispatchers need.

불이야! = alarm cry to make people move. 불이 났어요 = factual report to describe what is happening. 119에 신고해 주세요 = direct bystanders to call the emergency line. All three serve different moments in the same emergency.
불이야! (bare alarm) → 불났어요! (존댓말 report) → 불이 났어요! (fuller report) → 주방에서 불이 났어요 (location added). Always pair the alarm with 나가세요 ('get out') to direct people.

Saying bare 불 does not work as an alarm — 불 is just the noun 'fire/flame/light'. Saying 불야! also fails because 불 ends in ㄹ (a consonant), so the exclamatory ending must be 이야: 불이야!. Mixing in English as '불 알람!' is also not Korean.

mistakes: Shouting just 불 to mean 'Fire!'
불 alone is the noun 'fire/light' and sounds incomplete as an alarm. Use the set cry 불이야! or 불났어요!
Saying 불 알람! for 'Fire!'
That mixes English 'alarm' and is not idiomatic. Koreans shout 불이야!
Writing 부리야 or 불이얌.
It's 불 + 이야 = 불이야!. Keep the ㄹ on 불 and the plain 이야 ending.

usage: I'm lost (lit. I lost the road)
존댓말 to a passerby, shop staff, or anyone who can help
반말 to a friend or family on the phone
-어버리다 stresses the loss is total and you feel helpless
It's my first time here, so I don't really know the way
Softer framing that explains why you're lost without sounding panicked
examples: 저… 실례지만 길을 잃었어요. 혹시 도와주실 수 있어요?
Um… excuse me, I'm lost. Is there any chance you could help?
Polite opener to a stranger; 실례지만 ('excuse me for bothering you') is the ideal softener before admitting you're lost
A: 왜 이렇게 늦어? / B: 미안, 길을 잃었어. 지금 찾아가고 있어.
A: Why are you so late? / B: Sorry, I got lost. I'm finding my way now.
반말 A/B exchange; 찾아가다 = 'to make one's way to a place'
지하철역에서 나왔는데 길을 잃었어요. 이 주소 어떻게 가요?
I came out of the subway station and got lost. How do I get to this address?
Real situation: show the address on your phone while asking; 어떻게 가요? = 'how do I get there?'
nuance: 길을 잃었어요 literally says 'I lost the road' — 길 (road/way) is the object, so it takes the object marker 을, and 잃다 (to lose) is conjugated in the past because the loss has already happened. This particle is crucial: it is 길을 잃다, never 길이 잃다 or 길에 잃다. Adding the completive suffix -어버리다 (길을 잃어버렸어요) intensifies the sense of hopelessness, as if you've truly wandered into nowhere and can't recover on your own. The nearest alternative, 여기가 어디예요? ('where is this?'), only asks your location — it doesn't explain your predicament or invite extended help; fluent speakers often combine both in one breath: 길을 잃었어요. 여기가 어디예요? The follow-up questions — 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요? ('is there a subway station nearby?') or 이 주소 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to this address?') — are what unlock practical help. English speakers often say 나는 잃어버렸어요 (no object — 'I lost something' with nothing named) or mark 길 with the wrong particle, such as 길이, because in English 'I' is the subject; in Korean, 길 (the road) is the grammatical object of 잃다.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I lost the road' (길을 잃다). Korean frames being lost as having lost your path — 길 is the object with 을, not the subject. The past tense 잃었어요 reflects that the losing already happened, which is how Korean describes a current state that resulted from a past action.

존댓말 잃었어요 is for any stranger or helper. 반말 잃었어 is for friends or family on the phone. Soften the approach to a stranger with 저기요 (excuse me) or 실례지만 before launching into 길을 잃었어요 — Korean conversation openers matter, even in distress.

여기가 어디예요? only asks where you are — a single factual question. 길을 잃었어요 describes your whole situation and signals you need sustained help. Experienced Korean speakers often pair both: 길을 잃었어요. 여기가 어디예요? for the most complete plea.
길을 잃었어 (반말) → 길을 잃었어요 (존댓말) → 길을 잃어버렸어요 (completive, more helpless). The -어버리다 version is the most emotionally expressive and is common in speech.

Saying 나는 잃어버렸어요 with no object leaves Koreans wondering what you lost. You must keep 길을 as the object. Also, 잊었어요 (from 잊다 'to forget') is a different word entirely — 'I forgot the road' is not 'I got lost'.

mistakes: Saying 나는 잃어버렸어요 with no object.
잃어버리다 needs an object. To mean 'I'm lost', say what was lost — the way: 길을 잃었어요.
Using the wrong particle: 길이 잃었어요 or 길에 잃었어요.
잃다 takes the object marker. It must be 길을 잃었어요.
Saying 길을 잊었어요.
잊다 is 'to forget'; 잃다 is 'to lose'. Being lost is 길을 잃었어요, not 잊었어요.

usage: 존댓말 to staff, police, or any passerby who might help
반말 to a friend or family on the phone
분실하다: the formal/written word used at a lost-and-found counter or police desk
I think my wallet was stolen
도둑맞다 when you suspect deliberate theft, not just accidentally dropping it
examples: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요. 혹시 못 보셨어요?
I lost my wallet. Have you seen it by any chance?
Bare report to a café or shop staff; 혹시 ('by any chance') softens the question and signals you don't assume blame
A: 어디 있었어? / B: 택시에 지갑 두고 내렸어. 잃어버렸어.
A: Where were you? / B: I left my wallet in the taxi and got off. I lost it.
반말 A/B; 두고 내리다 = 'to leave behind and get off a vehicle'
저 여기 카페에서 지갑을 잃어버렸어요. 분실물 센터가 있나요?
I lost my wallet here at the café. Is there a lost-and-found?
Real situation: asking about the 분실물 센터 (lost-property desk) is the next practical step
nuance: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 = 지갑 (wallet) + 을 (object marker) + 잃어버리다, where the completive suffix -어버리다 adds the nuance that the loss is total and the speaker feels genuine regret — which is why Koreans almost always use 잃어버리다 rather than bare 잃다 when talking about a missing personal belonging. At a police desk or lost-property counter, the formal equivalent 분실하다 is expected: 지갑을 분실했어요. The critical distinction: 잃어버리다 implies you accidentally misplaced or dropped the wallet (your fault or bad luck), while 도둑맞다 or 도난당하다 means someone stole it — police need to know which, because the report form and the investigation differ. If you were pickpocketed, say 지갑을 소매치기당했어요 or 도난당했어요. English speakers often say just 잃었어요 (sounds abruptly clipped), drop the object marker, or say 지갑이 잃어버렸어요 with the subject particle — but the wallet is the object of losing, so 지갑을 is mandatory.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'I lost-and-it's-gone my wallet' — the suffix -어버리다 marks the action as complete and regretted, which is why it almost always replaces bare 잃다 when talking about a personal belonging. The real meaning is both a factual report and an expression of distress.

존댓말 잃어버렸어요 for any stranger or official. 반말 잃어버렸어 for friends/family. At a formal counter (police desk, lost-and-found, airline desk) use the Sino-Korean 분실하다: 지갑을 분실했어요. This is the register cue that you understand the procedure.

잃어버리다 = accidentally misplaced (you don't know where it went). 도둑맞다 = stolen by someone (implies a criminal). 도난당하다 = same as 도둑맞다 but more formal/written. Police and insurance forms require you to specify which — a mistake here changes the entire paperwork.
지갑을 잃었어요 (clipped, less natural) → 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 (standard, with regret) → 지갑을 분실했어요 (formal) → 지갑을 도둑맞았어요 (stolen). Pair with 분실물 신고 (lost-property report) or 분실물 센터 (lost-and-found).

Dropping the object marker (지갑 잃어버렸어요) is fine in fast speech but can sound unclear when reporting to an official. The bigger error is 지갑이 잃어버렸어요 with the subject particle — the wallet is the object being lost, so 지갑을 is required.

mistakes: Using 지갑이 잃어버렸어요.
The wallet is the object of 잃어버리다, so use 을: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.
Saying 지갑을 잃어버렸어요 when it was clearly stolen.
잃어버리다 implies you misplaced it. If stolen, say 지갑을 도둑맞았어요 or 도난당했어요.
Confusing 지갑 with 가방.
지갑 is a wallet/purse; 가방 is a bag. Name the right item: 지갑을 잃어버렸어요.

usage: 존댓말 to police, embassy staff, or hotel concierge
반말 to a friend or family member you're calling for advice
분실하다 at a police station, embassy desk, or formal written report
I need to get my passport reissued
재발급 받다: the natural follow-up phrase you'll need at the embassy
examples: 여권을 잃어버렸어요. 어떻게 해야 돼요?
I lost my passport. What should I do?
Bare report plus 어떻게 해야 돼요? ('what should I do?') — the most useful opener because it invites guidance from staff or the police
A: 언제 마지막으로 봤어요? / B: 호텔 체크아웃 때 봤는데 그 이후로 없어요.
A: When did you last see it? / B: I had it at hotel checkout but haven't seen it since.
A/B exchange with a police officer; 체크아웃 때 = 'at checkout time'
여권을 잃어버려서 대사관에 가야 하는데, 경찰 신고부터 해야 하나요?
I lost my passport so I need to go to the embassy — should I report to the police first?
Real situation; 신고부터 해야 하나요 = 'should I report first?' — asking about the procedure correctly
nuance: 여권을 잃어버렸어요 = 여권 (passport, Sino-Korean: 旅券, lit. 'travel document') + 을 + 잃어버리다. Losing a passport abroad is a chain of bureaucracy — hotel, police, then your embassy — so you'll say this phrase multiple times, always in 존댓말, and switch to the formal 여권을 분실했어요 at official desks where the word 분실 (loss/misplacement) triggers the right paperwork. Police will ask whether it was lost (잃어버리다) or stolen (도둑맞다 / 도난당하다), because a stolen passport triggers an Interpol notice while a lost one triggers a reissue (재발급) process — the difference matters legally. The next phrase you need is 여권 재발급 신청을 하고 싶어요 ('I'd like to apply for passport reissuance') or simply 여권 재발급 받아야 해요. English speakers confuse 여권 with 여건 (conditions/circumstances) because the two words sound similar, and they often drop the object marker 을 in a formal report — keep it for clarity.

structuredNuance.t: 여권 (旅券, 'travel document') + 을 + 잃어버리다. The Sino-Korean 여권 is the only standard word for passport. The -어버리다 suffix signals the loss is total and regretted — exactly the emotional reality when your passport is gone abroad.

존댓말 잃어버렸어요 to hotel staff, police, fellow tourists. Switch to 분실했어요 at a police desk or embassy — that word signals you understand the formal procedure. Never use 반말 잃어버렸어 to officials. At the embassy ask for 여권 분실 신고서 (passport loss report form).

잃어버리다 = misplaced/lost accidentally. 도난당하다 = stolen. The Korean police form requires you to choose one — a passport stolen by a pickpocket needs 도난당했어요, which triggers a criminal report and an alert to immigration authorities. Don't use 잃어버렸어요 if it was taken from you.
여권을 잃어버렸어요 → 여권을 분실했어요 (formal) → 여권 재발급 받아야 해요 (next step) → 여권 분실 신고서를 작성하고 싶어요 (I'd like to fill out a loss report).

여권 and 여건 (conditions/circumstances) sound very similar — a slip here will completely confuse your listener. Listen carefully: 여-권 (旅券) vs 여-건 (與件). Also, dropping the object marker in a formal report (여권 잃어버렸어요) sounds casual; keep 여권을 for clarity.

mistakes: Saying 여건을 잃어버렸어요.
여건 means 'circumstances/conditions'. A passport is 여권: 여권을 잃어버렸어요.
Dropping the object marker: 여권 잃어버렸어요 in a formal report.
In casual speech 을 can drop, but for a clear official report keep it: 여권을 잃어버렸어요.
Using 잃어버렸어요 when it was stolen.
If stolen, the police need 여권을 도둑맞았어요 / 도난당했어요, which triggers a different report.

usage: 존댓말 request to a bystander or shop staff
반말 to a friend in a sudden crisis; 좀 softens the urgency slightly
Could you please call the police?
More formal and polite — when you have a moment to be composed
112 is Korea's police number; 신고하다 = 'to report a crime to authorities'
examples: 경찰을 불러 주세요! 저 사람이 제 가방을 훔쳤어요!
Please call the police! That person stole my bag!
Bare urgent request; 훔치다 = 'to steal' — cleaner and more precise than just 가져가다
A: 무슨 일이에요? / B: 싸움이 났어요. 빨리 경찰 좀 불러 주세요!
A: What's happening? / B: There's a fight. Please quickly call the police!
A/B exchange showing how the phrase fits into a real frantic moment; 싸움이 나다 = 'a fight breaks out'
사고가 났어요. 다친 사람이 있어요. 경찰이랑 구급차 좀 불러 주세요!
There's been an accident. Someone is hurt. Please call the police and an ambulance!
Real scene combining both services; 경찰이랑 구급차 = 'police and ambulance'
nuance: 경찰을 불러 주세요 = 경찰 (police) + 을 + 부르다 (to call/summon) + 주세요. The verb choice is important: 부르다 means to summon someone to your location — it's the same verb you use to call a taxi (택시를 부르다) or beckon a person over. This is different from 전화하다 (to make a phone call to), which you'd use for 112에 전화해 주세요. The real-world distinction between the two: 부르다 = bring the police here; 112에 전화하다 or 신고하다 = contact the police by phone or formally report the incident. Korea's police line is 112 (not 911, which doesn't exist in Korea); fire and ambulance is 119. Mixing up 112 and 119 in an emergency wastes critical seconds. English speakers often say 경찰에게 전화해 주세요 ('please phone the police'), which is grammatically fine but less natural as a shout than the summon verb 불러 주세요. Another pitfall: 경찰을 불어 주세요 — that's from 불다 ('to blow'), not 부르다 ('to call/summon').

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please call/summon the police (here)'. The verb 부르다 means to summon to your location — the same word used for calling a taxi. The real meaning is: get law enforcement to arrive at this spot right now.

존댓말 경찰을 불러 주세요 to any bystander, staff, or passerby. 반말 경찰 불러 줘 to a friend. The polished 경찰 좀 불러 주시겠어요? is for calmer moments — a dispute, not an assault. In the heat of the moment, bare 경찰 불러 주세요! is correct and fully natural.

경찰을 불러 주세요 = summon the police to come here (focus on their presence). 112에 신고해 주세요 = formally report the incident by calling 112 (focus on filing a report). In a theft or fight, both are useful: shout 경찰 불러 주세요! first, then 112에 신고하다 afterward.
경찰 불러 줘 (반말) → 경찰을 불러 주세요 (존댓말) → 경찰 좀 불러 주시겠어요? (formal polite) → 112에 신고해 주세요 (phone report). Korea: 112 = police, 119 = fire + ambulance.
경찰을 전화해 주세요 is wrong — 전화하다 never takes 을/를 before the institution you're calling; you need 에 (경찰에 전화해 주세요). Also, 경찰을 불어 주세요 is wrong — 불다 means 'to blow'; the summon verb is 부르다 → 불러.

mistakes: Calling 119 for police.
119 is fire and ambulance. Police is 112: 112에 신고해 주세요.
Using 경찰을 전화해 주세요.
전화하다 never takes 을/를. To phone the institution use 에 (경찰에 전화해 주세요 / 112에 전화); to summon them here, use 부르다: 경찰을 불러 주세요.
Saying 경찰을 불어 주세요.
The verb is 부르다 → 불러, not 불어 (which is 불다 'to blow'). Correct: 경찰을 불러 주세요.

usage: 존댓말 request to bystanders; 좀 softens the urgency into a natural appeal
반말 to a friend in a sudden emergency
Could you please call an ambulance?
Polite formal version — slightly less urgent in tone
119 dispatches both ambulances and fire trucks in Korea; 전화하다 = 'to phone'
examples: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요! 사람이 쓰러졌어요!
Please call an ambulance! Someone collapsed!
Bare urgent cry; 쓰러지다 = 'to collapse' — the most important context word to know
A: 할아버지가 가슴이 아프대요. 어떻게 해요? / B: 빨리 119에 전화해! 구급차 불러!
A: Grandpa says his chest hurts. What do we do? / B: Quickly call 119! Call an ambulance!
반말 A/B family crisis exchange; 가슴이 아프다 = 'chest hurts' — always potentially serious
여기 사람이 의식이 없어요. 빨리 구급차 좀 불러 주세요! 저는 CPR 할게요!
Someone here is unconscious. Please quickly call an ambulance! I'll do CPR!
Real scene; 의식이 없다 = 'is unconscious'; 'CPR 할게요' signals you're taking action while others call
nuance: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 = 구급차 (救急車, lit. 'emergency-relief vehicle') + 좀 + 부르다 + 주세요. 구급 (救急) means 'emergency relief/first aid' and 차 means 'vehicle' — so 구급차 is literally an emergency-relief car. As with the police, you summon an ambulance with 부르다 (to call/summon to this location), not 전화하다 (to phone). The 좀 is not really 'a little' here; in spoken Korean 좀 added to a request smooths out the urgency so it doesn't sound like a bark — it's a pragmatic softener that native speakers use even in genuine crises. In practice, 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 and 119에 전화해 주세요 are near-synonyms in emergency situations; the second is more specific about the action (dial the number). Korea's emergency number is 119 for fire and ambulance — not 911 as in the US, and not 112 which is police. English speakers sometimes say 앰뷸런스 (the loanword), which Koreans understand but it sounds foreign and may slow comprehension with a frightened bystander; native 구급차 is clearer and faster to process.

structuredNuance.t: 구급차 = 救急車, literally 'emergency-relief vehicle' (구급 = emergency relief + 차 = vehicle). The real meaning of the full phrase is: summon an ambulance to arrive here immediately. 좀 is a pragmatic softener, not literal 'a little'.

존댓말 불러 주세요 to any bystander or stranger. 반말 불러 줘 to a friend in panic. The softener 좀 stays in both registers — it makes the request sound human rather than a command. For phoning 119 yourself, say 여기 구급차가 필요해요 ('we need an ambulance here') to the dispatcher.

구급차 좀 불러 주세요 = summon the vehicle here (action-focused). 119에 전화해 주세요 = call the emergency line (phone-focused). 응급실이 어디예요? = find the ER room (travel-focused, if the person can move). In the worst cases, you shout the first two and leave the third for later.
구급차 좀 불러 줘 (반말) → 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 (존댓말) → 119에 전화해 주세요 (dial the number). 응급 처치 (emergency treatment) and 응급실 (ER) are the related terms you'll need next.

앰뷸런스 is understood but slows comprehension. Use 구급차. A critical number mistake: Korea is 119 for ambulance/fire, NOT 911 (US) or 999 (UK). 112 is police only. Getting the number wrong in an emergency can cost minutes.

mistakes: Dialing 911 or 112 for an ambulance.
In Korea, ambulance and fire are 119. Police is 112. Say 119에 전화해 주세요.
Using 구급차를 전화해 주세요.
To summon it, use 부르다: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요. To phone the number, say 119에 전화해 주세요.
Confusing 구급차 (ambulance) with 구급상자 (first-aid kit).
구급상자 is a first-aid box. You need the vehicle: 구급차 좀 불러 주세요.

usage: 존댓말 to a bystander; 119 = fire + ambulance dispatch center
반말 to a friend in an emergency
신고하다 stresses that you are officially reporting an emergency, slightly more formal
Quick, get 119 on the line — call an ambulance!
빨리 (quickly) + 좀 emphasizes both speed and urgency
examples: 빨리 119에 전화해 주세요! 불이 났어요!
Quickly call 119! There's a fire!
Bare urgent command to a bystander; pairs 119에 전화 with 불이 났어요 naturally
A: 사람이 쓰러졌어요! / B: 제가 119에 전화할게요! 움직이지 마세요!
A: Someone collapsed! / B: I'll call 119! Don't move them!
A/B showing task distribution in a crisis; 움직이지 마세요 = 'don't move (the person)'
사람이 차에 치였어요. 119에 신고하고 움직이지 마세요! 제가 신고할게요!
A person got hit by a car. Call 119 and don't move them! I'll report it!
Real scene; 치이다 = 'to get hit by a vehicle'; 신고할게요 = 'I will report it' — taking ownership is natural in Korean emergency response
nuance: 119에 전화해 주세요 = 119 + 에 (destination particle 'to') + 전화하다 (to phone) + 주세요. The particle 에 is not optional here: 전화하다 marks the number you call with 에 ('phone TO a number'), never 를 or 에서. Korea's 119 is a combined fire-and-ambulance dispatch line — not the police (112), and not 911 or 999, which do not exist in Korea. Knowing this single number can be the most important piece of Korean in a medical or fire emergency. The distinction between 전화하다 and 신고하다 is subtle: 전화해 주세요 = 'phone the number' (action-focused); 신고해 주세요 = 'formally report the emergency' (report-focused, sounds slightly more official). In the field both are used interchangeably. The digits 119 are read in Korean as 일일구 (il-il-gu), not as English 'one one nine'. English speakers also reach for 911 out of habit, and some use the wrong particle (119를 전화해 주세요 or 119에서 전화해 주세요 — both wrong).

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'please phone to 119'. The particle 에 marks the destination of a phone call — you call TO a number. The real meaning is: contact Korea's combined fire-and-ambulance emergency line right now.

존댓말 전화해 주세요 to a bystander or stranger. 반말 전화해 줘 to a friend. The more formal 신고해 주세요 is also correct and slightly more official-sounding. If you call 119 yourself, say 여기 불이 났어요 or 여기 사람이 쓰러졌어요 plus your location immediately — dispatchers are trained for this.

119에 전화해 주세요 = dial the number (action). 구급차 좀 불러 주세요 = get an ambulance to arrive here (result). 119에 신고해 주세요 = officially report the emergency (formality). All three are correct in emergencies; 119에 전화해 주세요 is the most concise and universally understood.
119에 전화해 줘 (반말) → 119에 전화해 주세요 (존댓말) → 119에 신고해 주세요 (formal report). Always read 119 as 일일구 in Korean. 112 = police only.

Three compounding errors: (1) dialing 911 instead of 119 — there is no 911 in Korea; (2) wrong particle — 119를 전화해 주세요 is wrong; use 119에; (3) reading the digits as English 'one one nine' — Korean dispatchers expect 일일구.

mistakes: Saying 119를 전화해 주세요.
전화하다 marks the destination with 에: 119에 전화해 주세요.
Calling 911 instead of 119.
Korea uses 119 for fire/ambulance and 112 for police. There is no 911.
Reading 119 as English 'one one nine'.
Read the digits in Korean: 일일구 (il-il-gu).

usage: 존댓말 to staff, a taxi driver, or a passerby; subject marker 이 after consonant-final 응급실
반말 to a friend who knows the area
어디 있어요? is an equally polite variant, slightly more explicit
가장 가까운 ('nearest') added when speed matters and you're not at a hospital yet
examples: 저기요, 응급실이 어디예요? 빨리 가야 해요.
Excuse me, where is the emergency room? I need to go quickly.
Bare question with urgency cue; 빨리 가야 해요 communicates the seriousness to whoever you ask
A: 지금 어디야? / B: 병원 안인데 응급실 어디야? / A: 1층이야, 빨리 와!
A: Where are you now? / B: I'm inside the hospital — where's the ER? / A: First floor, come quick!
반말 A/B exchange between friends rushing to hospital; 1층 = first floor
애가 열이 너무 높아요. 가장 가까운 응급실이 어디예요? 밤에도 문 여나요?
My child's fever is very high. Where's the nearest emergency room? Is it open at night too?
Real scene; 문 열다 = 'to be open'; asking about night hours is critical for emergency visits
nuance: 응급실이 어디예요? = 응급실 (emergency room, Sino-Korean: 應急室, lit. 'emergency office-room') + 이 (subject marker after consonant) + 어디예요 ('where is it?'). Korean asks 'where is the ER?' by making 응급실 the subject of the question — not the object — which is why you must use the subject marker 이 and cannot say 응급실을 or 응급실를. For a true life-threatening emergency, calling 119 and letting them dispatch is usually faster than finding the ER yourself; ask 응급실이 어디예요? when you're already mobile and the patient can be transported by yourself or a taxi. The distinctions that save confusion: 응급실 = the hospital's ER for walk-in emergencies; 병원 = hospital or clinic in general; 약국 = pharmacy for minor ailments. To ask a taxi driver, just say 응급실이요! and the hospital name if you know it. English speakers sometimes say 어디 있어요? without the subject marker (fine in casual speech), or confuse 응급실 with 응급 (just the adjective prefix), or pronounce it 응급식 — but it ends in ㄹ: 응급실 (eung-geup-sil).

structuredNuance.t: 응급실 (應急室) literally means 'emergency response room'. 이 is the subject marker after the consonant ㄹ. 어디예요 = 'where is (it)?'. The question makes 응급실 the subject: 'where is the emergency room (as a place that exists)?'

존댓말 어디예요 to any stranger, staff, or taxi driver. 반말 어디야 to friends. Add 가장 가까운 ('nearest') when you need to find one urgently and are not at a hospital. To a taxi driver, 응급실 빨리요! ('ER, quickly!') plus the hospital name is the most urgent form.

응급실 = the ER (for serious emergencies and walk-in crises). 병원/의원 = clinic or hospital for regular medical care. 약국 = pharmacy (for minor issues, no prescription needed for many things). 119를 부르다 = call 119 and be dispatched (faster than finding the ER yourself in a real crisis).
응급실 어디야 (반말) → 응급실이 어디예요? (존댓말) → 응급실이 어디 있어요? (어디 있어요 variant) → 가장 가까운 응급실이 어디예요? (nearest). Also useful: 야간 응급실 있어요? ('is there a night ER?').

응급실을 어디예요? is wrong — 어디예요 takes the subject particle, not the object. Also: 응급 (the Sino-Korean prefix meaning 'emergency') is not a standalone noun for ER; you need the full 응급실. And the pronunciation ends in -실 (sil), not -식 (sik).

mistakes: Saying 응급실을 어디예요?
어디예요 takes the subject marker, not the object: 응급실이 어디예요?
Confusing 응급실 with 병원 or 약국.
응급실 = ER, 병원 = hospital/clinic, 약국 = pharmacy. Name the one you need.
Pronouncing 응급실 as 응급식.
It ends in ㄹ: 응급실 (eung-geup-sil). 응급식 is not a word.

usage: 존댓말 to any stranger, 119 dispatcher, or medical staff
반말 to a friend or family member
격식 -습니다 when reporting to officials, police, or 119
다친 사람 ('a hurt/injured person') when reporting about someone else, not yourself
examples: 저 다쳤어요. 무릎을 다쳤어요.
I'm hurt. I hurt my knee.
Bare report naming the body part; 무릎을 다치다 = 'to injure one's knee' — the body part takes 을/를
A: 괜찮아요? / B: 아니요, 넘어져서 발목을 다쳤어요. 걷기가 힘들어요.
A: Are you okay? / B: No, I fell and hurt my ankle. It's hard to walk.
A/B exchange; 넘어지다 = 'to fall down'; 발목 = ankle; 걷기가 힘들다 = 'hard to walk'
계단에서 굴러서 머리를 다쳤어요. 의식은 있는데 많이 아파요.
I rolled down the stairs and hurt my head. I'm conscious but in a lot of pain.
Real scene; 의식은 있다 = 'is conscious'; helps a 119 dispatcher assess severity immediately
nuance: 다쳤어요 is the past tense of 다치다 ('to get injured'), and Korean naturally frames an injury in the past tense because the injury event has already occurred — saying present 다쳐요 would mean 'I am in the process of injuring myself right now', which makes no sense. The body part that was injured takes the object marker 을/를: 무릎을 다쳤어요, 발목을 다쳤어요, 손을 다쳤어요. The critical distinction from 아파요 is cause and type: 다치다 describes an accidental physical injury (a fall, a cut, a collision), while 아프다 describes pain or illness from any source, including sickness. A broken bone from falling is 다쳤어요; stomach pain from food poisoning is 아파요. Note that even if an injury is very painful, you use 다쳤어요 to name the injury and 아파요 to describe the pain — both often appear in the same sentence: 무릎을 다쳤어요. 너무 아파요. English speakers often say present-tense 다쳐요 (wrong), use 아프다 for a wound (imprecise), or mark the body part with 이/가 instead of 을/를 (grammatical error).

structuredNuance.t: 다쳤어요 is the past tense of 다치다 ('to get injured'). Korean uses the past for an injury because the damaging event has already happened — the injury is a completed result, not an ongoing action. The real meaning is 'I have sustained a physical injury (from an accident)'.

존댓말 다쳤어요 to strangers, doctors, and 119. 반말 다쳤어 to friends. The formal 다쳤습니다 is used when reporting to police or in official statements. Adding the body part with 을/를 (무릎을 다쳤어요) is essential for medical staff to assess severity.

다치다 = physical injury from an external accident (fall, cut, collision). 아프다 = general pain or illness from any cause (sickness, cramps, headache, plus injury pain). A wound is 다쳤어요; the pain from that wound is 아파요. The two can coexist: 다쳤는데 아파요 ('I got injured and it hurts').
다쳤어 (반말) → 다쳤어요 (존댓말) → 다쳤습니다 (격식). With body part: 무릎을 다쳤어요, 손을 다쳤어요. For someone else: 다친 사람이 있어요 ('there's an injured person').

Using present-tense 다쳐요 for an injury that just happened sounds like 'I injure myself' (habitual/general) — always use the past 다쳤어요. Using 이/가 on the body part (무릎이 다쳤어요) is also wrong — 다치다 takes 을/를 on the body part.

mistakes: Saying 다쳐요 (present) for an injury that just happened.
Korean uses the past for a completed injury: 다쳤어요.
Using 아파요 to report a wound.
아프다 is general pain/illness. For an injury from an accident, say 다쳤어요.
Marking the body part with 이/가: 무릎이 다쳤어요.
다치다 takes the object marker on the body part: 무릎을 다쳤어요.

usage: The fixed crowd-alarm shout; register-free, used by anyone in theft shock
It's a thief! / There's a thief!
존댓말-flavored form when reporting more calmly to staff or security
저 사람 (that person over there) added to point out the culprit to others
소매치기: specifically for pickpocketing in a crowded place — more precise than 도둑
examples: 도둑이야! 잡아 주세요!
Thief! Please catch him!
Bare alarm immediately followed by 잡아 주세요 ('please catch him') — the two shouts that always go together
A: 제 핸드폰이 없어요! / B: 저 사람이 가져갔어요! 도둑이야! 잡아요!
A: My phone is gone! / B: That person took it! Thief! Catch them!
A/B exchange showing how bystanders respond; 가져가다 = 'took/carried off'
지하철에서 누가 제 지갑을 빼 갔어요. 소매치기야! 112에 신고해 주세요!
Someone slipped my wallet out on the subway. Pickpocket! Please call 112!
Real scene; 빼 가다 = 'to slip something out and leave'; 112 = police for crime reports
nuance: 도둑이야! is built from 도둑 (thief/burglar) + 이야 (exclamatory copula after a consonant), literally 'it's a thief!' — and like 불이야! it functions as a register-free alarm that any Korean shouts in the moment of shock, regardless of who is listening, because there's no time for politeness. The key structural rule: because 도둑 ends in a consonant (ㄱ), you must use 이야, not plain 야 (which follows a vowel). To report calmly to staff or write a statement, you switch to 도둑이에요 or 저 사람 도둑이에요. The lexical distinction: 도둑 is any thief or burglar; 소매치기 is specifically a pickpocket — the person who silently slips items from bags, pockets, or coats in crowded places. In a subway or market theft, 소매치기야! is the more accurate and useful alarm. After shouting, the natural sequence is 잡아 주세요! ('please catch them!') and calling 112 (police). English speakers try to shout bare 도둑 (incomplete as an alarm) or say 도적 (a more archaic literary word for 'bandit'), or attach the wrong exclamatory ending 야 instead of 이야.

structuredNuance.t: 도둑 (thief) + 이야 (exclamatory copula after consonant) = 'It's a thief!' The real function is a crowd alarm — the same register-free emergency shout as 불이야!. Anybody shouts this to everybody, overriding normal politeness entirely.

도둑이야! is register-free in the moment of shock. Once the immediate chaos passes, switch to 도둑이에요 or 저 사람 도둑이에요 for a composed report to staff or police. For a written statement or police report, describe the incident: 지갑을 소매치기당했어요 or 가방을 도둑맞았어요.

도둑 = a thief or burglar (general term). 소매치기 = specifically a pickpocket (silent theft of items from pockets/bags in crowds). 강도 = a robber who uses force or threat. Use the right word: 소매치기야! in a subway, 강도야! if someone threatened you with force.
도둑이야! (alarm) → 도둑이에요! (composed report) → 저 사람 도둑이에요 (pointing out the culprit) → 소매치기야! (pickpocket alarm). Always follow with 잡아 주세요! and call 112.

Bare 도둑! sounds incomplete as an alarm — the 이야 ending is what turns it into a shout. Saying 도둑야! is wrong because 도둑 ends in a consonant (ㄱ): the ending must be 이야, not 야. 도적 is literary/historical Korean, not a street cry.

mistakes: Shouting just 도둑.
As an alarm it's incomplete. The set cry is 도둑이야! (or polite 도둑이에요).
Using 도둑야 instead of 도둑이야.
After a consonant the ending is 이야: 도둑이야!. 야 follows a vowel.
Saying 도둑 for a pickpocket on the subway.
A pickpocket is 소매치기. Shout 소매치기야! when someone slips something out of your bag.

english: Where is this? / Where am I?
usage: 존댓말 to a passerby when you don't know where you are
반말 to a friend you're calling or texting
어디인가요 — a touch softer and more formal, like asking a shop owner or elder
Where exactly am I right now?
Longer form that spells out the first-person perspective — used when genuinely disoriented
examples: 저기요, 여기가 어디예요? 처음 와봐서요.
Excuse me, where is this place? It's my first time here.
Pair with the explanatory -서요 ending which gives a reason naturally; 처음 와봐서요 = 'because it's my first visit'
A: 어디야? 왜 안 와? / B: 택시에서 내렸는데 여기가 어디야? 길을 잃었어.
A: Where are you? Why aren't you here? / B: I got out of the taxi but where is this? I got lost.
반말 A/B; combines 여기가 어디야? with 길을 잃었어 — the two companion phrases natives use together
휴대폰 배터리가 나갔어요. 여기가 어디예요? 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요?
My phone died. Where am I? Is there a subway station nearby?
Real scene; 배터리가 나가다 = 'battery dies'; combining location question with the follow-up need
nuance: 여기가 어디예요? = 여기 (here/this place) + 가 (subject marker after vowel) + 어디예요 ('where is it?'), literally 'where is here?' — which is exactly how Korean frames 'where am I?'. The subject particle is 가 (not 이) because 여기 ends in a vowel. This is a location-centered question: Korean grammar focuses on the place rather than the person, unlike English 'where am I?' which centers the self. Because of this, the English-speaker instinct to say 나는 어디예요? ('where am I as a person?') sounds bizarre in Korean — as if asking what category of thing 나 (I) belongs to. The natural companion to this phrase is 길을 잃었어요 — saying both gives a more complete picture and invites practical help rather than just a map pointer. The useful follow-ups are 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요? ('is there a subway station nearby?') or 이 주소 어떻게 가요? ('how do I get to this address?'). To ask about a remote location, use 거기가 어디예요? (거기 = there); 여기 is strictly 'here'.

structuredNuance.t: 여기 (here) + 가 (subject marker) + 어디예요 ('where is it?') = literally 'where is here?' Korean frames the PLACE as the subject, not the person. Saying 나는 어디예요? ('where am I?') sounds like asking what type of thing 나 is — not natural. The correct form centers the location: 여기가 어디예요?

존댓말 여기가 어디예요? to any stranger, passerby, or shop owner. 반말 여기가 어디야? on the phone to a friend. Open the conversation with 저기요 ('excuse me') to a stranger before asking. 지금 제가 어디에 있는 거예요? is the most explicit and thorough version for when you're truly disoriented.

여기가 어디예요? = single factual question about your current location. 길을 잃었어요 = full explanation of being lost that invites extended help. Native speakers often chain both: 길을 잃었어요. 여기가 어디예요? — losing the road is the cause, not knowing where you are is the result.
여기가 어디야? (반말) → 여기가 어디예요? (존댓말) → 여기가 어디인가요? (polite formal) → 지금 제가 어디에 있는 거예요? (explicit, disoriented). Often followed by 이 근처에 지하철역 있어요? or 이 주소 어떻게 가요?

나는 어디예요? is the direct calque of 'where am I?' — but Korean centers the place, not the person. Use 여기가 어디예요? Also, the particle must be 가 (not 를): 여기를 어디예요? is wrong because 어디예요 needs the subject, not an object.

mistakes: Saying 나는 어디예요? for 'Where am I?'
Korean asks about the place: 여기가 어디예요?, literally 'where is here?'
Using 여기를 어디예요?
어디예요 takes the subject marker: 여기가 어디예요?
Confusing 여기 (here) and 거기 (there).
Ask about where you are with 여기; 거기/저기 point elsewhere.

usage: 존댓말, the standard polite way to flag your limited Korean to any stranger
반말 to a friend or peer your age
I do not speak Korean well
격식 -습니다; 한국말 is the slightly more colloquial word for the language
The essential follow-up request — always pair this with 잘 못해요 when asking someone to accommodate you
examples: 죄송해요, 한국어를 잘 못해요.
I'm sorry, I'm not good at Korean.
The most natural opener; 죄송해요 cushions the admission and invites the other person's patience
A: 주문하시겠어요? / B: 저 한국어를 잘 못해요. 혹시 영어 되세요? / A: 조금요!
A: Are you ready to order? / B: I'm not good at Korean. Do you happen to speak English? / A: A little!
Real A/B restaurant exchange; 혹시 영어 되세요? is a natural, gentle way to ask
한국어를 잘 못해요. 죄송한데 조금만 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요?
I'm not good at Korean. Sorry, but could you speak just a bit more slowly?
Real scene; 조금만 ('just a little') + 천천히 + 말씀해 주시겠어요 is the full polite request to slow down
nuance: 한국어를 잘 못해요 = 한국어 (Korean language) + 를 (object marker) + 잘 (well) + 못하다 (to be unable to do well). The key interpretive point: 잘 못하다 means 'can't do it well' (ability is limited), while 안 하다 means 'I don't do it' (by choice). Using 안 하다 — 한국어를 안 해요 — implies you are refusing or unwilling, which is not what you mean. The 잘 softens the claim from 'I can't speak Korean at all' (한국어 못해요) to 'I'm not good at it', which is more accurate and humble. 한국어 is the neutral/formal word for the language, while 한국말 is more colloquial and warm; both are correct. The classic follow-up toolkit: 천천히 말씀해 주세요 ('please speak slowly'), 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요? ('could you say that again?'), and 영어 하시는 분 계세요? ('is there anyone who speaks English?'). English speakers most often get the particle wrong (한국어가 잘 못해요 — the language is the object, not the subject) or write 잘못해요 as one word, which means 'to do something wrong/make a mistake' — a completely different word.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'cannot do Korean well' — 잘 (well) + 못하다 (cannot do). The real meaning is 'my Korean ability is limited', which is a polite, humble admission rather than a flat refusal. 잘 is the crucial modifier that makes this sound honest rather than helpless.

존댓말 잘 못해요 for any stranger, service staff, official, or elder. 반말 잘 못해 for friends. 격식 잘 못합니다 for more formal settings. Always pair this phrase with the follow-up request: 천천히 말씀해 주세요 or 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요?

한국어를 잘 못해요 ('not very good') vs 한국어를 못해요 ('can't speak Korean at all') — the 잘 makes it softer and more accurate. 한국어를 안 해요 ('I don't do Korean') sounds like a choice or refusal and is the wrong phrase. 한국어를 배우고 있어요 ('I'm learning Korean') is the positive alternative.
한국어 잘 못해 (반말) → 한국어를 잘 못해요 (존댓말) → 한국어를 잘 못합니다 (격식) → 한국어가 서툴러요 (lit. 'clumsy at Korean', softer alternative). Follow with 천천히 말씀해 주세요 or 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?

Two critical errors: (1) 잘못해요 written as one word means 'to do something wrong / make a mistake' — completely different. Always write 잘 못해요 with a space. (2) 한국어가 잘 못해요 uses the wrong particle — Korean is the object of 못하다, so 한국어를 is required.

mistakes: Saying 한국어를 안 해요.
안 하다 = 'choose not to do'. To say you lack ability, use 못하다: 한국어를 잘 못해요.
Using the subject particle: 한국어가 잘 못해요.
The language is the object of 못하다: 한국어를 잘 못해요.
Splitting 못해요 wrongly or writing 잘못해요.
Here 못 means 'cannot' (잘 못해요 = can't do well). 잘못하다 as one word means 'to do wrong / make a mistake' — a different meaning.

english: Is there anyone who speaks English?
usage: Is there anyone who speaks English?
존댓말 with double honorific — 분 (honorific for person) + 계세요 (honorific for 있다) — correct when addressing a group of strangers
반말 to friends; plain 하는 사람 + 있어 — casual, fine among equals
영어 하실 수 있는 분 계신가요?
Is there someone who can speak English?
More formally polite — 하실 수 있는 + 계신가요 — at a service counter or in a formal setting
Direct question to one specific person; 할 줄 알다 = 'to know how to do'
examples: 혹시 영어 하시는 분 계세요?
Is there by any chance anyone who speaks English?
혹시 ('by any chance') is the essential softener — it signals you don't assume anyone will help and makes the request feel less demanding
A: 여기 영어 하시는 분 계세요? / B: 네, 제가 조금 할 수 있어요. 뭐가 필요하세요?
A: Is there anyone here who speaks English? / B: Yes, I can speak a little. What do you need?
A/B exchange; B's response 조금 할 수 있어요 ('I can speak a little') is the most common reply
죄송한데, 영어 하시는 분 계세요? 제가 한국어를 잘 못해서요.
Sorry, is there anyone who speaks English? It's because my Korean isn't very good.
Real scene; -서요 trailing explanation ('because…') is natural and polite; pairs directly with 한국어를 잘 못해요
nuance: 영어 하시는 분 계세요? deploys two layers of honorific simultaneously: 분 (the honorific word for 'person', vs plain 사람) and 계세요 (the honorific existence verb, vs plain 있어요). Both are necessary when you're addressing a room full of strangers or asking staff — Koreans notice if you undercut the register by saying 사람 있어요? to an elder or manager. The verb for using a language in Korean is 하다 (to do/speak), not 말하다 or 말해요: you say 영어 하다, 영어 하시다, 영어 할 줄 알다. The dividing line between 계세요? and 할 줄 아세요?: 계세요? scans a group ('is there someone who…?'); 할 줄 아세요? is a direct question to one identified person in front of you. The softener 혹시 ('by any chance') before the question is nearly obligatory in polite speech — without it, the question can feel like a demand. English speakers often say 영어 말해요? (calquing 'speak English' with 말하다) or use plain 사람 있어요? to an official context, both of which under-register the respect the situation calls for.

structuredNuance.t: 영어 (English) + 하시는 (honorific relative clause 'who speaks') + 분 (honorific 'person') + 계세요 (honorific 'is there?'). Literally 'is there a person (honorific) who speaks English (honorific)?'. The double honorific is not redundant — both are socially required when addressing a group of strangers.

Use the double-honorific form 하시는 분 계세요? with any group of strangers, at service counters, hospitals, or hotels. Reduce to 하는 사람 있어? only with peers or friends. Always add 혹시 at the start to soften. If a specific person is in front of you, switch to the direct 영어 할 줄 아세요?

영어 하시는 분 계세요? = scans a group for any English speaker. 영어 할 줄 아세요? = asks one specific person. 영어 되세요? = casual-polite shorthand ('does English work for you?'), common in service contexts like restaurants. All three are correct in different frames.
영어 하는 사람 있어? (반말) → 영어 하시는 분 계세요? (존댓말 group) → 영어 하실 수 있는 분 계신가요? (formal polite) → 영어 할 줄 아세요? (direct to one person) → 혹시 영어 되세요? (service-context shorthand).

영어 말해요? calques 'speak English' with 말하다, but Korean uses 하다 for languages. 영어 말하시는 분 계세요? is intelligible but unnatural. Also, 사람 있어요? to a manager or elder is under-polite — always use 분 + 계세요 with strangers in a service context.

mistakes: Using 사람 있어요? to elders or staff.
To a roomful of strangers the honorific 분 + 계세요 is more courteous: 영어 하시는 분 계세요?
Saying 영어 말해요? for 'speak English'.
Korean uses 하다 for languages: 영어 하시는 분, or 영어 할 줄 아세요? for one person.
Using 있으세요? wrongly here.
For 'is there a person', the honorific existence verb is 계세요 (people exist with 계시다): 영어 하시는 분 계세요?

usage: 존댓말 reporting any accident to 119, bystanders, or police
반말 to a friend or family member
격식 -습니다 when reporting formally to police, insurance, or in a written statement
교통사고 (traffic accident) specifies a vehicle crash — the word dispatchers need to send the right unit
examples: 사고가 났어요! 사람이 다쳤어요!
There's been an accident! Someone is hurt!
Bare report paired with 사람이 다쳤어요 — the two pieces of information a dispatcher needs first
A: 여기 교통사고가 났어요. / B: 지금 어디예요? / A: 강남대로 3번 출구 앞이요.
A: There's been a car accident here. / B: Where are you now? / A: In front of exit 3 on Gangnam-daero.
A/B exchange with a 119 dispatcher; giving the exact location immediately is critical
고속도로에서 사고가 났어요. 차가 두 대 부딪혔어요. 다친 사람이 있어요. 119 좀 불러 주세요!
There's been an accident on the highway. Two cars collided. Someone is hurt. Please call 119!
Real scene; 부딪히다 = 'to collide'; 두 대 = 'two (vehicles)'; full three-sentence report is the 119 template
nuance: 사고가 났어요 = 사고 (accident, Sino-Korean: 事故) + 가 (subject marker) + 나다 ('to break out/occur') in the past tense. Korean uses the verb 나다 for events that 'break out' — the same verb as 불이 나다 ('a fire breaks out') and 문제가 나다 ('a problem arises'). The grammatical key: the accident is the subject of 나다 (사고가 났어요), so the subject marker 가 is required — you cannot say 사고를 났어요 (that would need 사고를 일으켰어요 = 'caused an accident'). The specificity: 사고 = any accident; 교통사고 = specifically a traffic/vehicle accident; 산업재해 = workplace accident. For a 119 call, lead with 교통사고가 났어요 or 사람이 쓰러졌어요 so dispatchers immediately route correctly. If you were the victim, use 사고를 당했어요 ('I was in an accident', literally 'I received an accident') — this centers the victim's experience, unlike 사고가 났어요 which is a neutral third-person report. English speakers say 사고를 만들었어요 ('I made an accident') — accidents aren't 'made' in Korean; they 'break out' with 나다.

structuredNuance.t: 사고 (事故, accident) + 가 (subject marker) + 나다 ('to break out/occur'). Literally 'an accident broke out'. Korean uses 나다 for uncontrolled events that erupt — fires, accidents, problems. The accident is the grammatical subject, not an object; 나다 is intransitive here.

존댓말 났어요 for 119 calls, bystanders, and initial reports. 반말 났어 to family or friends. 격식 났습니다 for official statements, insurance reports, or police interviews. When phoning 119, follow immediately with 위치 ('location') — dispatchers always ask 어디예요? first.

사고가 났어요 = neutral report: an accident occurred (no blame assigned, no victim identified). 사고를 당했어요 = victim-centered: I was involved in/affected by an accident. 사고를 냈어요 = 'I caused an accident' (you are at fault). These three carry completely different legal weight — use the right one.
사고 났어 (반말) → 사고가 났어요 (존댓말) → 사고가 났습니다 (격식) → 교통사고가 났어요 (specific: vehicle) → 사고를 당했어요 (victim frame) → 사고를 냈어요 (I caused it).

사고를 만들었어요 ('made an accident') is wrong — accidents 나다 ('break out'), not 만들다 ('make/create'). Also: 사고를 났어요 is wrong; 나다 requires the subject marker: 사고가 났어요. And 사고를 냈어요 (transitive causative) means you CAUSED it — don't use this unless you are admitting fault.

mistakes: Saying 사고를 만들었어요 for 'there was an accident'.
Accidents 'occur' with 나다, not 'are made'. Say 사고가 났어요.
Using 사고를 났어요.
With 나다 the accident is the subject: 사고가 났어요. (Use 사고를 당했어요 if you want 'I had an accident'.)
Saying just 사고 to a dispatcher.
Specify what kind for the right response: 교통사고가 났어요 for a car crash.

usage: 존댓말 to a doctor, pharmacist, nurse, or any bystander
반말 to a friend or family member
격식 -습니다 in a formal report or medical intake form
Name the body part + 가/이 (subject marker) + 아파요 — the standard template for all body-part pain
examples: 저 좀 아파요. 약국이 어디예요?
I'm feeling a bit sick. Where is the pharmacy?
Bare statement paired with the natural follow-up; 좀 softens the admission and 약국이 어디예요? is the first practical step for mild illness
A: 왜 그래? / B: 어제부터 머리가 너무 아파. 열도 있는 것 같아.
A: What's wrong? / B: My head has been really hurting since yesterday. I think I have a fever too.
반말 A/B; 어제부터 = 'since yesterday'; 열이 있다 = 'to have a fever' — the full clinical picture in two sentences
배가 너무 아파요. 토할 것 같아요. 병원에 가야 할까요?
My stomach really hurts. I feel like throwing up. Should I go to a doctor?
Real scene; 토할 것 같다 = 'feel like vomiting'; 병원에 가야 할까요? = 'should I go to the hospital?' — a full self-triage question
nuance: 아파요 is the polite conjugation of 아프다, a single Korean adjective that covers both 'to be in pain' and 'to be sick/ill' — one word handles what English splits between 'hurt' and 'sick'. To name the body part that hurts, that part becomes the grammatical subject with 가/이: 배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요, 목이 아파요, 무릎이 아파요. Note the irregular conjugation: 아프다 has a ㅡ-irregular stem; 아프 + 아요 → the ㅡ drops → 아파요, not 아프아요. The dividing line from 다쳤어요 is cause and type: 아프다 = pain or illness from any source (infection, stomachache, headache, muscle soreness); 다치다 = physical injury from an external accident (a fall, a cut, a collision). Both can describe the same body part at the same time: 넘어져서 무릎을 다쳤어요. 무릎이 아파요 ('I fell and hurt my knee; my knee hurts'). The follow-up toolkit: 병원에 가야 해요 ('I need to go to a clinic'), 약국이 어디예요? ('where's the pharmacy?'), 진통제 주세요 ('please give me painkillers'). English speakers say 배를 아파요 (object marker 를 on the body part) — but 아프다 is an adjective and the painful body part is its subject: 배가 아파요.

structuredNuance.t: 아파요 = polite form of 아프다, literally 'am painful/sick'. It covers both 'it hurts' and 'I'm sick' — Korean does not split these meanings. The body part that hurts is the subject with 가/이 (배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요), not the object.

존댓말 아파요 to any stranger, medical staff, or pharmacist. 반말 아파 to friends and family. 격식 아픕니다 on medical forms or formal reports. At a 119 call or emergency, describe the body part and severity: 가슴이 너무 아파요 ('my chest hurts a lot') tells the dispatcher it may be cardiac.

아프다 (pain or illness from any cause: cold, stomachache, injury pain) vs 다치다 (physical injury from an accident). A headache is 머리가 아파요. A bruise from a fall is 다쳤어요. The pain FROM a bruise is 아파요. You need both words; one describes the injury event, the other describes the sensation.
아프다 → 아파요 (존댓말) → 아파 (반말) → 아픕니다 (격식). With body parts: 배가 아파요, 머리가 아파요, 목이 아파요, 다리가 아파요. The ㅡ drops in conjugation: 아프 + 아요 → 아파요.

The most common error is 배를 아파요 — treating the body part as an object with 를. But 아프다 is an adjective (descriptive verb) and the aching part is its subject: 배가 아파요. Also, 아프요 (skipping the irregular contraction) is wrong — the correct form is 아파요.

mistakes: Marking the body part with 을/를: 배를 아파요.
The hurting part is the subject of 아프다: 배가 아파요.
Writing 아프요 instead of 아파요.

For a wound from a fall or cut, use 다쳤어요; 아파요 is general pain/illness.
